source.title: Negative Pre-activations Differentiate Syntax
source.authors: Linghao Kong; Angelina Ning; Micah Adler; N. Shavit

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates causal roles of selected neurons in syntax, but does not test the claim versions about the share of neurons with nameable jobs, canonical Inception neurons, attribution graphs, or explanation accuracy on held-out activations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron ablations and neuron-level analyses of syntactic differentiation. These findings concern neuron function but do not measure the job-share or explanation claims in V1–V7. Results cited from earlier work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study selects high-Wasserstein-distance neurons, ablates only their negative pre-activations, and measures grammar and other benchmarks. It never estimates what share of neurons have one nameable job. It does not examine InceptionV1 or compare architectures or tools by interpretable share. It builds no attribution graphs and does not score explanations against held-out activations. Its argument that positive-activation-only analyses miss computation touches on V4 and V6 in spirit but reports no measure of either.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that negative pre-activations of a sparse set of Wasserstein neurons are a functional substrate for syntax. Sign-specific ablation damages BLiMP/TSE far more than matched controls. Perplexity-matched low-WD ablations instead hurt non-grammatical benchmarks more, giving a double dissociation. They urge interpretability methods to attend to negative activation regions. They make no claim about the share of neurons with single jobs.
record.recipe_differences: The study selects neurons using Wasserstein distance or mapping difficulty and clamps negative pre-activations, then measures grammar and other benchmark performance; it does not use the audit or explanation-testing recipe described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The effects vary by model, layer, and ablation selection. The study reports stronger grammatical degradation in Llama and Mistral than in Qwen; early-layer perturbations have larger grammatical effects; and selection by mapping difficulty instead of Wasserstein distance gives a qualitatively similar result.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing negative pre-activations of the top 1% WD neurons sharply lowers TSE accuracy in Llama (84.4 to 55.2) and Mistral (84.6 to 54.6), with smaller drops in Qwen. Random and perplexity-matched controls leave grammar mostly intact. Selected Wasserstein neurons in Pythia separate syntactic tokens via negative-negative differentiation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A sparse subpopulation of high-WD neurons in smooth-activation LLMs uses the negative pre-activation region for syntax, so neuron interpretation based on positive activations alone may miss function.

record.problems: The analyses focus on selected high-WD neurons rather than estimating the prevalence of interpretable neurons. The token-pair examples are qualitative and do not test explanations on held-out activations. The authors note a structural confound in the negative-clamping analysis: the intervention disproportionately collapses negative-negative pairs, so correlations between those pairs and grammatical vulnerability may partly reflect the intervention mechanics. Some appendix and layerwise results are presented in figures without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: perplexity results, non-grammatical benchmark results, POS-level token surprisal, layerwise grammar results, activation-function variants, WD-versus-MD validation, and checkpoint-level WD/TSE tracking. These are reported in Sections 2–4 and Appendices A.1–A.6 but do not measure any of V1–V7 or add a distinct neuron-job result beyond the included grammar and token-differentiation rows.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles; Qwen3 8B Base is used only for ablations.
No job-share estimates for any model or scale.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis; superposition is only cited.
No comparison of interpretable-neuron share across architectures, regularization or tools. The ReLU vs GELU contrast concerns pre-activation distribution shape only.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
Argues that negative activations are neglected but does not test explanation prediction on held-out firing.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Rows r15/r16 are marked 'partial' for Qwen perplexity-matched controls (BLiMP 82.5 to 81.3; TSE 84.8 to 82.4). These states describe the study's own effect, not any version. The paper's critique of positive-activation-centric interpretation is conceptually adjacent to V6, but no explanation-accuracy data are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit the proportion of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one or more jobs, or the share not understood.
Does not measure job-share similarity across models or scale up to trillion-parameter models.
Does not analyze the canonical InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or test recursive generalization against superposition.
Does not compare interpretability shares across architectures, regularization, or explanation tools.
Does not build attribution graphs or compare their behavioral explanations with a replacement model or reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations written from activating examples predict held-out firing.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Pythia 1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Selected the top ten most differentiated token pairs for neuron 5176 and inspected their pre-activation signs and token categories.

conditions.value: WikiText 2 validation; 2,000 random tokens arranged in 1,000 pairs
top ten by normalized output-distance/input-distance ratio

rows.measure: sign pattern and linguistic character of differentiated pairs
rows.value: Eight of the top ten pairs were driven to two distinct negative pre-activation values; the pairs were described as predominantly grammatical, including a preposition/determiner example.
rows.note: This is a qualitative case study, not a held-out explanation test or a measure of the share of interpretable neurons.

rows.subject: Pythia 1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Classified the signs of the most differentiated input pairs for top-MD neurons by layer.
rows.measure: proportion of negative-negative, positive-negative, and positive-positive pairs
rows.value: Negative-negative pairs were at least 30% in all layers except layer 1; positive-positive pairs were comparatively rare.
rows.note: The paper does not provide exact proportions in the text.

rows.subject: Pythia 1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Tracked pair-sign composition among the most differentiated pairs of the same entangled neurons over training.
rows.measure: frequency of negative-negative, positive-negative, and positive-positive pairs
rows.value: Negative-negative pairs rapidly became prevalent during training, while positive-positive pairs remained a small fraction and positive-negative pairs decreased.
rows.note: Exact proportions are not stated in the text.

rows.subject: Pythia 1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Clamped negative pre-activations of 5% of Wasserstein neurons and measured grammatical error.
rows.measure: error increase and its relationship to cohort mean WD
rows.value: Error increase had a strong positive relationship with mean WD; random and perplexity-matched controls showed little to no correlation.
rows.note: The paper gives a qualitative relationship rather than a numerical correlation in the text.

source_check.problem: Minor: the text also reports the same result for TSE (Fig. 7d), but the row covers BLiMP only.

relation.reason: Discusses neuron-level interpretability and polysemanticity, and gives qualitative neuron case studies (Sec. 5, A.5). Never measures or uses any version.

tranche.reason: Sign-specific ablation of Wasserstein neurons for syntax. No share of interpretable neurons, no InceptionV1, no attribution graphs, no explanation scoring; tests and uses no version.

source_check.notes: Rows r9 and r17 misstate the intervention uncertainty (the text gives ± 0.1). Qwen's 1% WD BLiMP drop (82.5 to 80.6) is only 0.7 below its PPL-matched control (81.3); the paper still calls it a large drop. Neuron interpretability evidence is qualitative only (Fig. 6, A8).
